publication_type: Engineering-oriented topic synthesis combining classroom IoT case studies, system reviews, official sensor-use guidance, and current commercial module documentation.
country_and_climate: The design is intended for classrooms across mixed climates, from naturally ventilated warm rooms to mechanically ventilated temperate classrooms. The variable selection stays stable across climates, but installation height, outdoor baselines, enclosure heating, and intervention logic must be climate- and building-specific.
objective_and_research_question: The objective is to specify and validate a low-cost classroom IoT node that distinguishes direct measurement from proxy channels and can be defended technically in a TCC. The practical research question is which commercial sensor modules and supporting architecture give the best trade-off among evidence quality, cost, power, maintenance burden, connectivity, and classroom relevance for each target variable.
study_design: This synthesis is a practical design-and-validation blueprint informed by classroom deployments, broad indoor-air sensor reviews, official QA/QC guidance, and current module specifications. It prioritizes variables and modules with stronger evidence and treats exploratory variables as optional add-ons rather than mandatory parts of the baseline node.
educational_context: The target use case is a fixed room node for ordinary classrooms in basic or higher education, installed for continuous monitoring during occupied periods and used to support ventilation, comfort, and maintenance decisions. The node must be easy to replicate room by room, simple to power and mount, and understandable to school operators who are not sensor specialists.
sample_and_duration: For validation, a staged pilot is recommended: bench testing of all assembled nodes, 7 to 14 days of pre-installation collocation, 2 to 6 weeks of pilot classroom deployment with event logs, and a shorter post-pilot recheck. This duration is long enough to expose occupancy cycles, power and network failures, cleaning events, and the first signs of drift without making the TCC schedule impractical.
environmental_variables: Recommended core variables are true CO2 for ventilation screening, air temperature and relative humidity for comfort and compensation, and PM1 plus PM2.5 for particle exposure and filtration decisions. Secondary or exploratory variables are PM10, illuminance, environmental noise, VOC or NOx indexes from MOX sensors, and occupancy or people-presence channels. Gas-specific CO, NO2, O3, or formaldehyde channels should only be added if there is a concrete use case and validation path.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: The node becomes much more useful when outdoor context is available. At minimum, the project should log weather and school schedule. If feasible, one outdoor or corridor reference node should capture CO2 baseline, outdoor PM episodes, and broad thermal context. Without that context, intervention logic can be wrong, especially for natural ventilation under polluted outdoor conditions.
occupancy_and_activity: Classroom interpretation depends heavily on occupancy pattern. Even if the node does not include a direct occupancy sensor, it should ingest timetable metadata and allow annotation of class periods, breaks, cleaning, and unusual activities. If people-presence is a design goal, direct sensing should be preferred over inference when privacy and budget allow.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: The node is intended to support manual or semi-automated operational decisions about windows, HVAC, and portable filtration. Validation should therefore document ventilation mode, window state, and whether air cleaners or noisy fans are operating, because these are not background details; they are part of the measurement regime that gives the data meaning.
spatial_granularity: The baseline recommendation is one fixed node per classroom at breathing-zone height, with extra temporary nodes only for pilot mapping or problem diagnosis. This keeps cost and maintenance manageable while preserving the room-level resolution that most school decisions require. Large halls, labs, or rooms with strong gradients may need more than one point to avoid misleading single-node interpretation.
sensor_specification: Recommended module set for the core node: true CO2 by Sensirion SCD41 or Senseair Sunrise; temperature and RH by SHT45 if not already provided acceptably by another direct sensor; PM by SEN55 as the strongest integrated low-cost option or PMS5003-class hardware as a cheaper alternative; illuminance by OPT3001; noise by ICS-43434-class digital MEMS microphone; exploratory VOC or NOx index by SGP41; and occupancy by a separate PIR for coarse presence or mmWave for stronger seated-presence detection. The selection is intentionally conservative: direct and selective modules are preferred for the core channels, while integrated proxy outputs are kept secondary.
calibration_and_qaqc: Node validation should be built into the project plan from day one. Every assembled node should receive an acceptance checklist covering power integrity, sensor detection, firmware version, timestamp behavior, local storage, and startup stabilization. Pre-deployment collocation should compare all core channels against one better reference or trusted instrument. After installation, the node should be checked again in situ, and the project should maintain QA flags for warm-up, missing data, clock resync, communication dropout, saturation, and any manual correction applied. Auto-calibration features such as automatic baseline correction must be documented and justified before they are enabled in persistent occupancy spaces.
acquisition_and_data_quality: A practical acquisition regime is native sensor sampling with 1 minute persisted aggregates for dashboards and analysis. CO2 and T/RH can be read once per minute or every few minutes; PM should sample continuously with minute aggregation; lux can sample every 10 to 60 seconds; and acoustic metrics can be computed on edge and uploaded as 1 minute summaries. The node should timestamp locally, buffer through outages, and report completeness and uptime as first-class outputs.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Lifecycle expectations differ by channel. SHT45-class sensors are usually stable for years, while PM modules require more cleaning and may suffer fan wear or fouling. CO2 modules are typically multi-year devices but remain sensitive to enclosure and calibration choices. Optional gas channels and occupancy peripherals add more points of failure than the core environmental stack.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: Recommended practical matrix by variable: CO2 ventilation marker, direct measurement, NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR, SCD41 preferred for compact low-power integration and Sunrise as a strong alternative; temperature and RH, direct measurement, SHT45-class digital sensor; PM1 and PM2.5, inferred optical mass from light scattering, SEN55 preferred when budget allows and PMS5003-class sensors acceptable for lower-cost trend monitoring; PM10, same optical family but only as a cautionary secondary output; illuminance, direct photopic lux, OPT3001 or equivalent; environmental noise, direct acoustic pressure with calibrated MEMS microphone and LAeq processing; VOC or NOx, exploratory proxy, SGP41 class index output only; occupancy, direct presence if needed, PIR for coarse presence and mmWave for better seated occupancy, with schedule-plus-CO2 inference only as a fallback proxy.
useful_output_and_units: Core outputs should be CO2 in ppm, air temperature in degrees C, RH in percent, PM1 and PM2.5 in micrograms per cubic meter, plus QA flags. Secondary outputs can include PM10 in micrograms per cubic meter, lux, LAeq in dBA, VOC Index, NOx Index, occupancy state, and estimated count if a direct occupancy channel is added. The node should avoid generic composite scores as its primary exported variables.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: The node should make this distinction explicit in firmware, schema, and dashboard labeling. Direct channels are true CO2, temperature, RH, illuminance, and calibrated acoustic pressure-derived metrics. Proxy or inferred channels are PM mass from optical scattering, VOC or NOx indexes from MOX sensing, PM10 from compact optical modules, and occupancy inferred from schedule or environmental data. This distinction is one of the core design decisions because it protects the TCC from overclaiming.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: CO2 should be measured selectively by NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR. T and RH use mature CMOS sensing. PM uses optical scattering and therefore depends on aerosol properties. Lux uses photopic photodiode response. Noise uses MEMS microphone pressure sensing with digital signal processing. SGP41-style gas sensing is broad-response MOX sensing and not selective chemistry. mmWave and PIR occupancy channels differ materially: PIR is movement-dependent, while mmWave can detect finer motion and persistent presence.
useful_range_and_real_performance: For real classrooms, the useful operating range is not the maximum sensor range but the range where the channel remains credible for school decisions. CO2 should cover outdoor baseline through severe under-ventilation events. T/RH should track ordinary comfort and moisture excursions without self-heating bias. PM should remain informative from low background to short classroom spikes. Lux should handle both low-light and strong daylight scenes. The design should favor modules with strong field behavior in that classroom regime over modules that simply advertise a broad nominal range.
operating_regime: The node should be mains powered and operate continuously, with local buffering and network retry. A practical default is 1 minute reporting, faster internal sampling where the sensor supports it, and occupied-period analytics at the dashboard layer. Duty cycling should be minimized for PM and exploratory gas channels because it complicates stabilization and interpretation. Warm-up exclusions should be encoded automatically after boot or reconnect.
interferences_and_confounders: The main confounders are thermal bias from the MCU, poor airflow around the enclosure, direct solar exposure, drafts from windows or HVAC, coarse dust bursts near PM inlets, vibration or airflow at the microphone port, and blind occupancy sensing geometry. Another major confounder is false semantic certainty: users often assume that more channels automatically mean more validity, when in practice each extra proxy channel can add noise and maintenance burden.
affordable_validation_protocol: A good TCC-level protocol has two phases. Phase 1, laboratory or bench acceptance: power test, timestamp test, duplicate agreement, and reference comparison for each channel that has an available instrument. Phase 2, field validation: collocate two or more nodes in one classroom or with one reference for 7 to 14 days, then deploy to separate classrooms with a documented timetable and event log. Minimum evidence for acceptance should include stable duplicates, interpretable drift, and post-installation checks. If occupancy sensing is included, add manual head counts for selected sessions.
validation_metrics: Required metrics are bias, MAE, RMSE, slope, intercept, correlation, uptime, missing-data fraction, and false-alert rate. For occupancy add accuracy, precision, recall, false-vacancy rate, and count MAE. For node engineering also report reboot rate, local-buffer recovery success, and timestamp consistency. The validation section should clearly separate channel accuracy from network reliability and from intervention usefulness.
installation_and_enclosure: Install the node at approximately seated head height with free airflow and away from windows, doors, direct sunlight, radiators, projectors, whiteboard solvent sources, and strong supply or return jets. The enclosure should be ventilated, should isolate heat-generating electronics from the sensing openings, and should preserve the intended flow path for the PM module and the intended acoustic exposure for the microphone. If a separate occupancy sensor is used, its mounting geometry should be documented independently from the environmental node.
hardware_integration: An ESP32-class MCU is a practical baseline because it supports Wi-Fi, I2C, UART, storage, and adequate compute for minute-scale edge logic. Core digital sensors integrate cleanly: SCD41, SHT45, SEN55, and OPT3001 use I2C, while PMS5003 uses UART and digital MEMS microphones use I2S. The node should include local flash or SD buffering, NTP synchronization, watchdog recovery, and a stable 5 V supply sized for PM current peaks. Optional occupancy or electrochemical gas channels should only be added if the extra integration complexity is justified by the research question.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] As of 2026-08-11, a practical low-volume core node with ESP32, SCD41, SHT45, and one PM sensor plus enclosure and power typically lands around USD 60 to USD 140 depending on whether the PM channel is PMS5003-class or SEN55-class. Adding lux and calibrated noise usually moves the room node into roughly USD 80 to USD 180. Adding mmWave occupancy or selective gas channels can push it beyond USD 200. A realistic TCC budget must also reserve money or access for validation instruments, spare parts, mounting, and maintenance.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity for the proposed node is strongest for the recommended core: true CO2, T/RH, and PM2.5. It is moderate for integrated noise and lux monitoring after local calibration. It is weaker for PM10, VOC or NOx proxy channels, and occupancy inference from environmental data alone. This maturity ranking should drive both the node scope and how strongly each channel is used in conclusions.
variable_specific_cautions: CO2 must be true CO2, not eCO2. T/RH can be biased badly by self-heating if the sensing head is not isolated. PM10 should not be oversold. VOC and NOx indexes from SGP41 are broad-response indicators and should not be treated as classroom pollutant concentrations. A MEMS microphone does not make the node a certified sound level meter. PIR does not count people and can miss still occupants. These cautions are design requirements, not only discussion points.
system_architecture: The recommended architecture is fixed classroom node to Wi-Fi to MQTT or HTTPS ingestion to a time-series database and a simple dashboard. The architecture should include device configuration, health telemetry, local buffering, and calibration metadata as part of the same pipeline. For small TCC scope, one broker and one dashboard stack are enough; the important requirement is that the stored data remain traceable to device, room, firmware, and calibration state.
connectivity_and_protocols: Wi-Fi is the default recommendation because it is simple, cheap, and adequate for minute-scale classroom telemetry. MQTT is preferable when the project wants lightweight message transport and easy device-state reporting; HTTPS is acceptable for simpler uploads. LoRaWAN is only attractive if mains power or Wi-Fi are unavailable, because it complicates high-frequency PM and acoustic summaries and usually reduces flexibility for QA metadata.
interoperability_and_data_model: The node should publish explicit fields for timestamp, room ID, node ID, variable, unit, QA flag, firmware version, and whether the channel is direct or proxy-derived. Extra metadata such as installation height, enclosure revision, and calibration version should be stored outside or alongside the time series. This schema is simple enough for a TCC and strong enough to keep later analysis reproducible.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: The node should use authenticated Wi-Fi credentials, encrypted transport where feasible, and a minimal attack surface. Room-level dashboards should not expose unnecessary user behavior detail. If the project adds occupancy sensing or retains any acoustic snippets, the privacy review becomes much stricter. The safest baseline is to avoid intelligible audio retention and to treat direct occupancy sensing as optional rather than default.
analytical_methods: The analysis layer should emphasize occupied-period summaries, duration above action bands, indoor-outdoor comparison where available, duplicate-agreement checks, and pre/post intervention comparisons. If occupancy is measured directly, occupancy-normalized ventilation analysis becomes stronger. Machine learning can be explored for secondary questions, but the core TCC should rely on interpretable statistics that are easy to defend.
derived_index_or_model: Useful derived outputs are excess CO2 above outdoor baseline, occupied-time above threshold, thermal excursion time, indoor-outdoor PM ratio, and occupancy-normalized exposure summaries. A composite classroom IEQ score is optional and should never replace the raw variable panels. If used, it must penalize proxy uncertainty rather than hiding it.
decision_rules_and_standards: Operational decision rules should combine direct measurements with persistence and context. Example classroom rules are repeated occupied CO2 peaks above approximately 1,000 ppm as a ventilation warning, more urgent follow-up when peaks repeatedly exceed approximately 1,500 ppm, RH excursions above roughly 60 percent for moisture concern, and PM actions based on persistence and outdoor context rather than one isolated spike. The rationale should cite WHO and ASHRAE positions and should state clearly which channels are direct and which are proxy.
intervention_and_automation: The node is best used for actionable but simple interventions: opening windows when outdoor air is cleaner, increasing outdoor air or purge periods, adding or tuning filtration, adjusting cleaning timing, improving shading or lighting scenes, and escalating persistent problems to facilities staff. Full closed-loop automation is possible but not necessary for a TCC. A better first target is trustworthy sensing plus human-readable recommendations.
environmental_outcomes: A successful node should reveal under-ventilated rooms, overheating patterns, PM episodes, and comfort trade-offs at room scale. Its value is that it turns classroom performance into something observable with enough temporal resolution to guide maintenance and operations rather than relying on occasional walkthroughs or perception alone.
health_and_learning_outcomes: The node does not measure health directly, but the selected variables have plausible links to comfort, symptom burden, attentional quality, and resilience when used to support interventions. The strongest claim the TCC can make is that better room-level observability supports earlier identification of conditions associated with poorer learning environments, not that the node alone proves educational or medical causality.
objective_subjective_integration: The design should leave room for short teacher or student annotations on stuffiness, glare, heat, or unusual noise. This is useful because measured traces and perceived experience do not always match. The best use of these subjective inputs is to interpret anomalies and to evaluate whether interventions were noticeable and acceptable.
quantitative_results: Current commercial modules provide a workable performance floor for a classroom node. SCD41 advertises a 400 to 5,000 ppm range, SHT45 advertises plus or minus 1 percent RH and plus or minus 0.1 degrees C typical accuracy, SEN55 integrates PM, T/RH, VOC, and NOx outputs in one module family, PMS5003 detects particles down to about 0.3 micrometers, and OPT3001 measures visible-light intensity over a wide lux range with photopic response. Classroom evidence also shows the operational value of dense monitoring: Hernandez and Canas demonstrated an integrated classroom device, while district and school studies show room-to-room heterogeneity large enough to justify fixed per-room sensing.
feasibility_and_acceptance: A node built around the recommended core stack is technically feasible, affordable for pilot scale, and understandable to non-specialists. Acceptance is usually highest when the interface stays simple and when the system is framed as building-performance support rather than staff or student monitoring. Each optional channel should therefore justify itself not only technically but operationally.
validity_and_limitations: The proposed node is valid for operational classroom monitoring, pilot studies, and intervention support, but it is not a substitute for regulatory monitoring or specialized research instruments. Single-point room measurement, proxy outputs, and climate-specific transfer all limit what can be claimed. The safest scope is a well-validated classroom node that supports decisions and generates reproducible evidence, not a universal all-in-one truth device.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The main contribution of this design is a practical and defensible selection hierarchy: prioritize true CO2, T/RH, and PM; add lux and noise only if they support the research question; treat VOC and occupancy inference carefully; and build QA/QC into the architecture. Key gaps remain in long-term classroom drift data, low-cost PM10 and VOC validation under real school use, and head-to-head comparisons of PIR, mmWave, and schedule-based occupancy context in ordinary classrooms.
